title: Man arrested after discussing plans for childcare mass shooting with [Claude]
content:
Sydney man allegedly discussed plans for childcare mass shooting with AI chatbot
A Sydney man threatened to carry out a mass shooting at a childcare centre in the city’s south during a conversation with a popular AI chatbot during which he referenced alleged Bondi Beach terrorist Naveed Akram, a court has heard.
David Lan Thackray was on Monday remanded in custody for a mental health assessment after Sutherland Local Court heard the 29-year-old told Claude, an AI-powered chatbot, that he planned to shoot several children at a childcare centre near his Hurstville home.
Thackray was on Sunday morning arrested after Interpol flagged his interactions with the chatbot and charged with using a carriage service to menace, harass or offend.
Prosecutors arguing to keep Thackray behind bars on Monday said there would be a “catastrophic” outcome if he was released and breached bail conditions imposed.
“What he intends to do is start murdering people in Sydney just like the [alleged] terrorist did in Bondi,” prosecutors told the court.
“We’re understanding what’s in his mind with his interactions with the chatbot.”
Naveed Akram remains in custody charged with murdering 15 innocent people and injuring dozens of others during an attack on the Chanukah by the Sea event at Bondi Beach last December. His father, Sajid Akram, was killed in the attack.
‘What he intends to do is start murdering people in Sydney just like the [alleged] terrorist did in Bondi.’The prosecution in court
According to a police facts sheet tendered to the court, Thackray allegedly told the chatbot he would “go down to the local Westfield right now and shoot up the local daycare”.
Thackray’s lawyer, Danilo Rajkovic, told the court his client had gone on a stress and frustration- induced tirade after trying to use the Claude platform to help treat an ear infection.
“There was no weight behind what he was saying,” Rajkovic said.
Thackray did not instruct the chatbot to issue threats to any person or organisation and believed he was having the interaction in the privacy of his own home, Rajkovic said.
Thackray had been using Claude’s voice mode, which allows users to have spoken conversations with the chatbot, the court heard. After receiving an email informing him that his Claude account had been suspended, Thackray requested to have the suspension reviewed.
Thackray, who is studying international relations, has no criminal history and has lived in Australia for more than 17 years, Rajkovic said.
Rajkovic said his client was confident detectives who seized his electronic devices on Sunday would find no evidence of radical indoctrination or ideological motivation.
Thackray will return to court pending the outcome of a mental health assessment.
Claude is an “AI assistant for life and work”, according to Anthropic, it’s provider.
The AI model is trained to refuse requests that involve planning or inciting violence and has automated safety systems to detect and block exchanges.
User data may be shared with law enforcement agencies where Anthropic believes it is necessary to prevent an emergency involving danger of death or serious physical injury to a person.

report.summary: A Sydney man was arrested after telling Anthropic's Claude, in voice mode, he planned a mass shooting at a childcare centre; Interpol flagged the chat.
report.background: Anthropic's Claude, like other major chatbots, is trained to refuse requests that involve planning violence and runs automated classifiers that scan conversations for imminent-threat signals. Anthropic's usage policy states user data may be shared with law enforcement where there is danger of death or serious physical injury, and the company publishes transparency reports on such disclosures. This case is notable because the escalation appears to have been triggered by the provider's own detection systems, then routed internationally through Interpol before NSW Police arrested the man on a Sunday morning. It lands months after the alleged Bondi Beach Chanukah-by-the-Sea attack, which killed 15 people and left Sydney unusually sensitive to mass-casualty threats, and as Australian regulators debate how AI assistants should handle violent ideation, mental-health distress and mandatory reporting duties.
key_points: David Lan Thackray, 29, of Hurstville, was arrested on Sunday after Interpol flagged his Claude interactions and charged with using a carriage service to menace, harass or offend. Sutherland Local Court remanded him in custody on Monday for a mental health assessment, with prosecutors arguing release would risk a 'catastrophic' outcome.

Police allege Thackray, using Claude's voice mode, said he would 'go down to the local Westfield right now and shoot up the local daycare' and referenced Naveed Akram, the man charged over the Bondi Beach attack. No threat was allegedly sent to any person or organisation.

Defence lawyer Danilo Rajkovic said his client was venting stress and frustration after trying to use Claude to help treat an ear infection, that 'there was no weight behind what he was saying', and that Thackray believed the exchange was private in his own home. He has no criminal history and had appealed an account suspension.

The case shows provider-side safety systems working as a detection layer: Anthropic suspended the account, and its policy permits sharing data with law enforcement to prevent death or serious injury. Prosecutors told the court the chatbot interactions were being used to understand what was in the man's mind.

The charges rest on Australian carriage-service law rather than a specific AI statute, and the international routing via Interpol raises untested questions about how chatbot flags cross borders, how quickly they are actioned, and what evidence survives from voice-mode conversations.
report.impact: The case sets an uncomfortable precedent: AI assistants are becoming an unofficial early-warning system for violence, with providers deciding when a private conversation becomes a police matter. For the industry, it sharpens pressure to document escalation policies, retain audio and text evidence defensibly, and publish disclosure counts — while inviting scrutiny over false positives and over-reporting of distressed or mentally unwell users. For developers, it highlights demand for moderation classifiers, logging pipelines and clear human-review paths, especially in voice products where tone and intent are harder to classify. For ordinary users, the practical lesson is that 'private' chats with hosted models are not confidential: safety systems read them, and serious threats can travel from a data centre to Interpol to a courtroom within days.
report.tools: To follow this space, watch the AI Incident Database (incidentdatabase.ai) for logged misuse cases, Anthropic's usage policy and transparency reporting, and open-weight guardrail models such as Llama Guard and Prompt Guard for building your own input/output classifiers. OpenAI's Moderation API and Azure AI Content Safety offer hosted alternatives, while HarmBench and similar evaluation suites let teams stress-test refusal behaviour. For policy context, the Partnership on AI and Australia's eSafety Commissioner publish guidance on AI, harm and reporting obligations.
